## What this document is, and what it is not

It is the **reference measurement** of plume, taken with a published and replayable instrument.
Every figure carries its qualifiers. Nothing is extrapolated: an empty cell is a
**not measured** cell, not an implicitly good one. When several runs coexist at the same
volume, they are ALL rendered: a run is never replaced by a more flattering one,
and the section "Measured gap between two runs" says which one describes the current code.

It is **not** a comparison with another product, nor a production measurement: it is a
synthetic bench with the **profile** of the production workload (see `bench/profile-prod.json`).

## Verdict — what these measurements allow to be claimed

Reference volume: **1,440,007 events** (`chaud-seul-v2@1.4M`), database **1434 MiB** encrypted with SQLCipher.

**On the 2 GiB budget — sustained.** Highest peak RSS measured across all cells: **1097 MiB**, i.e. **54 %** of the budget. And this is not a passive observation: the daemon ran under `MemoryMax=2G MemorySwapMax=0`, where an overrun is a kernel kill.

**What is FAST** (p50, window indicated, reference config):

- `C0-plancher` / all — **0.6 ms** (FLOOR: seek on a non-existent source (0 rows)), served by `raw`
- `C0-plancher` / au-dela-7d — **0.6 ms** (FLOOR: seek on a non-existent source (0 rows)), served by `raw`
- `C0-plancher` / 7d — **0.7 ms** (FLOOR: seek on a non-existent source (0 rows)), served by `raw`
- `C0-plancher` / 1h — **0.7 ms** (FLOOR: seek on a non-existent source (0 rows)), served by `raw`

**What is SLOW** — and these are the cases that the "on all fields" promise puts forward:

- `C6b-groupby-host` / 7d — **22.2 s** (group-by on host (as many groups as machines)), served by `raw`
- `C3c-groupby-json` / au-dela-7d — **21.8 s** (group-by on indexed EXTENDED field (action) + column), served by `raw`
- `C6b-groupby-host` / au-dela-7d — **20.9 s** (group-by on host (as many groups as machines)), served by `raw`
- `C3-groupby-hi` / all — **14.2 s** (group-by 3 high-cardinality dims (src_ip,host,source)), served by `raw`

**The disk was not used — and that is a limit, not good news.** Bytes read at the block layer, maximum over all cells: **0 MiB**. The database (1434 MiB) fits entirely in the machine's page cache (6839 MiB of memory available at minimum during the measurement). These latencies are therefore **bound by the CPU, not by storage**, and constitute a BEST CASE. At a volume where the database exceeds the available RAM, storage enters the equation — and that regime is not measured here.

**What these measurements do NOT allow to be claimed**:

- nothing beyond 1,440,007 events. The 10 M target was not reached by the real ingest path — not for lack of trying, but because the ingest throughput collapses with the volume already in the database, which the section "Where the collapse comes from" now ATTRIBUTES (and no longer assumes): the CPU cost per event rises, the daemon writes more and more bytes per row, and the write path is sequential. The remaining cost to reach 10 M is quantified there, as an arithmetic FLOOR on measured throughputs. Any latency announced at 10 M or 100 M would be an extrapolation, not a measurement.
- nothing on multi-tenancy (see the dedicated section). The cold tier, for its part, IS measured here — but only in `froid-actif@1.4M`, `froid-actif-v2@1.4M`, at a single hot window and a single volume: the other tables remain tables WITHOUT a cold tier.
- CONCURRENCY, for its part, is measured: up to 10 simultaneous analysts launching very large queries under the same enforced 2 GiB budget, with a check that the concurrent answer is IDENTICAL to the answer obtained alone (dedicated section).
- nothing on a deployment WITH masking from the empty-mask figures: the largest measured gap is **x239.5** on `C3b-groupby-routable` / all (152 ms empty mask against 36.3 s non-empty mask, `fts0-masque-vide@1.4M` against `fts0-masque-non-vide@1.4M` — two runs that differ ONLY by the mask).
  And masking does not ALWAYS go in the direction of slowing down: on `C4b-raw-deep` / all it is **x0.05**, hence FASTER (1055 ms empty mask against 54 ms non-empty mask, same number of rows returned). **The cause is NOT established by this measurement**, and it will not be invented. Two candidate mechanisms, each requiring a dedicated experiment to be told apart: (a) a mask placed on a high-cardinality dimension collapses it, fewer groups remain to aggregate — the query goes faster **because the answer changed**; (b) the masked run ran AFTER the unmasked run, hence on a warmer page cache. What would settle it: replay both runs in reverse order, and compare the results row by row. Meanwhile, the rule is simple — **a latency that drops in the presence of a mask must never be cited as a gain**.

##### Where the collapse comes from — measured attribution, not assumed

A falling throughput does not say WHY it falls. Three quantities say it, and
they are recorded at each tick by `bench/probe.py`:

- **Daemon CPU per event** — if it rises, the work per row really
  grows (deeper b-trees, indexes and FTS to maintain): it is the VOLUME.
- **CPU consumed by the rest of the machine** — it is CONTENTION. It includes
  the kernel threads that execute OUR own writes: so it is not
  only "other jobs", it is "CPU not billed to the daemon".
- **Bytes read at the block layer and cgroup memory stall** — if the 2 GiB ceiling
  forced the page cache to be reclaimed, they would rise. The budget is
  enforced by this same cgroup, and its page cache is billed to it.

| Rows in database | Throughput | Daemon CPU / event | daemon cores | cores of the rest | read at block layer | written / 1,000 ev. | memory stall | probe share |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 144,003 | 4,500 ev/s | 0.142 ms | 0.64 | 1.50 | 0 MiB | 4.3 MiB | 0 ms | 7.3 % |
| 372,003 | 3,076 ev/s | 0.216 ms | 0.66 | 1.81 | 0 MiB | 9.2 MiB | 0 ms | 21.3 % |
| 528,003 | 1,935 ev/s | 0.203 ms | 0.39 | 1.85 | 0 MiB | 11.3 MiB | 0 ms | 1.3 % |
| 648,003 | 1,875 ev/s | 0.266 ms | 0.50 | 1.98 | 0 MiB | 13.1 MiB | 0 ms | 7.4 % |
| 768,003 | 1,818 ev/s | 0.257 ms | 0.47 | 2.00 | 0 MiB | 14.7 MiB | 0 ms | 9.8 % |
| 852,003 | 1,411 ev/s | 0.323 ms | 0.46 | 2.08 | 0 MiB | 15.9 MiB | 0 ms | 10.6 % |
| 948,003 | 1,548 ev/s | 0.303 ms | 0.47 | 2.14 | 0 MiB | 16.6 MiB | 0 ms | 4.7 % |
| 1,032,003 | 1,200 ev/s | 0.438 ms | 0.53 | 2.01 | 0 MiB | 18.5 MiB | 0 ms | 1.2 % |
| 1,116,003 | 1,161 ev/s | 0.371 ms | 0.43 | 2.02 | 0 MiB | 18.8 MiB | 0 ms | 4.4 % |
| 1,212,003 | 1,142 ev/s | 0.401 ms | 0.46 | 1.94 | 0 MiB | 20.0 MiB | 0 ms | 28.0 % |
| 1,296,003 | 1,297 ev/s | 0.288 ms | 0.37 | 2.21 | 0 MiB | 19.7 MiB | 0 ms | 17.6 % |
| 1,368,003 | 837 ev/s | 0.603 ms | 0.51 | 1.94 | 0 MiB | 21.8 MiB | 0 ms | 30.7 % |

"Probe share" = what the sampler's ROW COUNT consumes of the interval: **7.4 % median**, **30.7 % worst**. This count is a scan served by the daemon: its cost is IN the CPU and throughput columns above. The net degradation of the product is therefore slightly smaller than the one shown — never larger.

Between 144,003 and 1,400,003 rows in the database, the throughput goes from **2,984 to 1,082 ev/s** (**÷2.76**) and the daemon CPU cost per event from **0.198 to 0.442 ms** (**×2.23**).

This drop FACTORISES, without remainder, into two measured factors — the throughput is exactly `busy cores / CPU per event`:

> **÷2.76** (measured throughput) = **×2.23** (CPU per event: the work per row grows with the b-trees) × **÷1.21** (cores busy with the daemon: 0.56 at the start against 0.47 at the end — it WAITS more). The product is ÷2.70, i.e. a 2 % gap with the measured drop: the gap is that of the per-quartile average, the identity `throughput = cores / CPU per event` being exact interval by interval.

The work per row therefore REALLY grows with the volume already in the database: it is the VOLUME, not the machine. And the daemon never occupies more than 0.66 core out of the 12 available: the write path is SEQUENTIAL, adding cores would change nothing.

The daemon occupies **0.47 core** at the median while the rest of the machine occupies **2.01** (12 cores available). The machine is therefore not saturated: the drop is not a contention for available CPU.

**What 10,000,000 events would cost**: at the LAST measured throughput (1,082 ev/s), 8,599,997 events would remain to be ingested, i.e. **2.2 h** — and that is a FLOOR, since the throughput has already been divided by 2.8 over the measured range and keeps falling. This row is arithmetic on measured throughputs, NOT a measurement at that volume: no latency in this document holds beyond the volume actually filled.

**Storage is not at fault on the READ side**: 0 MiB read at the block layer over the whole fill — the database fits in the page cache. **The 2 GiB ceiling does not slow things down through memory reclaim either**: 0.0 s of cumulative memory stall on the cgroup, measured.

Throughput over the sampled intervals: **min 837 ev/s, median 1455 ev/s, max 4500 ev/s**, for a `loadavg` ranging from 1.8 to 3.7. The gap of a factor 5.4 between the slowest and the fastest interval is no longer interpreted from the `loadavg`: the attribution subsection above breaks it down into daemon CPU, CPU of the rest of the machine and storage wait — three measured quantities.

The RSS column is the memory actually occupied by the daemon DURING the ingest — peak sampled here: **611 MiB**, to be set against the 2 GiB budget. It is a measurement, not an estimate.

> Scope of this curve: the sampler only covers the window during which it ran (144,003 to 1,400,003 rows). What happened before is not in this table, and is therefore not measured here.

Masking matters because it is **counter-intuitive**: a non-empty masking set
disarms the rollup route *and* the vectorised engine (`handlers/query.rs:282`,
`cold_store/planner.rs:601`). The confidentiality safeguard is a performance brake, so
figures published without this axis would only hold for a deployment **without** masking.
All cells are fired with the **same role** (`viewer`) in both states: a mask
rule at `role:''` does not constrain an admin (`field_filter.rs:110-115`), comparing it as
admin would measure nothing.

Latencies in milliseconds (wall, client side), unless marked `s`. `RSS` = real peak of the
process sampled every 15 ms during the query. `lu` = bytes read at the block layer by the
process (0 = served from the page cache).


**27 cells of this table have a `p95/p50` dispersion greater than 3.** On a shared machine, this does not describe plume: it describes the fact that the measurement was jostled by the other jobs. These cells are annotated; their `p50` remains usable, their `p95` does not.

**What `p95` is worth here**: 3, 7 repetitions per cell (the harness falls back to 3 when the first shot exceeds 3 s, so that the matrix stays tractable). At this number of samples, nearest-rank `p95` **is the maximum observed**: it is an upper bound on a tiny sample, not a real distribution tail. Read it as "the worst of N shots", nothing more.

Latencies in milliseconds (wall, client side), unless marked `s`. `RSS` = real peak of the
process sampled every 15 ms during the query. `lu` = bytes read at the block layer by the
process (0 = served from the page cache).


**32 cells of this table have a `p95/p50` dispersion greater than 3.** On a shared machine, this does not describe plume: it describes the fact that the measurement was jostled by the other jobs. These cells are annotated; their `p50` remains usable, their `p95` does not.

**What `p95` is worth here**: 3, 7 repetitions per cell (the harness falls back to 3 when the first shot exceeds 3 s, so that the matrix stays tractable). At this number of samples, nearest-rank `p95` **is the maximum observed**: it is an upper bound on a tiny sample, not a real distribution tail. Read it as "the worst of N shots", nothing more.

Latencies in milliseconds (wall, client side), unless marked `s`. `RSS` = real peak of the
process sampled every 15 ms during the query. `lu` = bytes read at the block layer by the
process (0 = served from the page cache).


**35 cells of this table have a `p95/p50` dispersion greater than 3.** On a shared machine, this does not describe plume: it describes the fact that the measurement was jostled by the other jobs. These cells are annotated; their `p50` remains usable, their `p95` does not.

**What `p95` is worth here**: 3, 7 repetitions per cell (the harness falls back to 3 when the first shot exceeds 3 s, so that the matrix stays tractable). At this number of samples, nearest-rank `p95` **is the maximum observed**: it is an upper bound on a tiny sample, not a real distribution tail. Read it as "the worst of N shots", nothing more.

Latencies in milliseconds (wall, client side), unless marked `s`. `RSS` = real peak of the
process sampled every 15 ms during the query. `lu` = bytes read at the block layer by the
process (0 = served from the page cache).


**37 cells of this table have a `p95/p50` dispersion greater than 3.** On a shared machine, this does not describe plume: it describes the fact that the measurement was jostled by the other jobs. These cells are annotated; their `p50` remains usable, their `p95` does not.

**What `p95` is worth here**: 3, 7 repetitions per cell (the harness falls back to 3 when the first shot exceeds 3 s, so that the matrix stays tractable). At this number of samples, nearest-rank `p95` **is the maximum observed**: it is an upper bound on a tiny sample, not a real distribution tail. Read it as "the worst of N shots", nothing more.

Latencies in milliseconds (wall, client side), unless marked `s`. `RSS` = real peak of the
process sampled every 15 ms during the query. `lu` = bytes read at the block layer by the
process (0 = served from the page cache).


**35 cells of this table have a `p95/p50` dispersion greater than 3.** On a shared machine, this does not describe plume: it describes the fact that the measurement was jostled by the other jobs. These cells are annotated; their `p50` remains usable, their `p95` does not.

**What `p95` is worth here**: 3, 7 repetitions per cell (the harness falls back to 3 when the first shot exceeds 3 s, so that the matrix stays tractable). At this number of samples, nearest-rank `p95` **is the maximum observed**: it is an upper bound on a tiny sample, not a real distribution tail. Read it as "the worst of N shots", nothing more.

Latencies in milliseconds (wall, client side), unless marked `s`. `RSS` = real peak of the
process sampled every 15 ms during the query. `lu` = bytes read at the block layer by the
process (0 = served from the page cache).


**33 cells of this table have a `p95/p50` dispersion greater than 3.** On a shared machine, this does not describe plume: it describes the fact that the measurement was jostled by the other jobs. These cells are annotated; their `p50` remains usable, their `p95` does not.

**What `p95` is worth here**: 3, 7 repetitions per cell (the harness falls back to 3 when the first shot exceeds 3 s, so that the matrix stays tractable). At this number of samples, nearest-rank `p95` **is the maximum observed**: it is an upper bound on a tiny sample, not a real distribution tail. Read it as "the worst of N shots", nothing more.

Latencies in milliseconds (wall, client side), unless marked `s`. `RSS` = real peak of the
process sampled every 15 ms during the query. `lu` = bytes read at the block layer by the

**What `p95` is worth here**: 3, 7 repetitions per cell (the harness falls back to 3 when the first shot exceeds 3 s, so that the matrix stays tractable). At this number of samples, nearest-rank `p95` **is the maximum observed**: it is an upper bound on a tiny sample, not a real distribution tail. Read it as "the worst of N shots", nothing more.

## Measured gap between two runs — `avant-leviers@1.4M` vs `apres-leviers@1.4M`

Comparison `avant-leviers@1.4M` -> `apres-leviers@1.4M`, SAME database, SAME instrument, SAME machine, consecutive runs. Both rows are measurements; the delta is their subtraction, nothing more.

**What changed between the two runs**: two fixes of the query path, measured here. (1) The budget guard now waits on a CONDITION (condvar with timeout) instead of polling a flag every 50 ms: it protects the same thing, at the same threshold, with the same interruption, but it no longer QUANTISES the latency — previously every reading was rounded up to the next multiple of 50 ms, and the guard was joined before the response was sent. It covers both execution gates: `run_on_conn` (/api/query) and `read_with_watchdog` (alerts, cases, freshness, sources, /api/search). (2) Whether cursor pagination applies is DERIVED from the properties of the wrap instead of a list of two commands, and a projected pipeline (`| table`/`| fields`) is now served by the cursor instead of silently falling back to OFFSET: this is the `C4d-keyset-projete` cell. Comparability caveat: these two runs use the SAME database, but AFTER the `event_fields_fts` fill of phase 3 (database 1434 MiB against 1263 MiB for the `fts0-*@1.4M` tables above) and on a much less loaded machine. They are comparable WITH EACH OTHER; they are not comparable with the tables of the first reference. Five cells go the other way (C1b/all +2.7 s, C5b/24h +632 ms, C5/all +467 ms, C2d/24h +252 ms): on these four the `SQL` column moves AS MUCH as the wall time, yet the fixes act ONLY on the wait AROUND the SQL — these are therefore long scans jostled by the machine, and they are left as they are.

Machine load recorded: `loadavg` 2.9–5.5 during the BEFORE run, 2.8–3.5 during the AFTER run. On a shared machine, a gap of a few milliseconds proves nothing; only clear-cut gaps are usable, and the cells whose dispersion is annotated above are to be read with the same reservation.

## Measured gap between two runs — `chaud-seul@1.4M` vs `froid-actif@1.4M`

Comparison `chaud-seul@1.4M` -> `froid-actif@1.4M`, SAME database, SAME instrument, SAME machine, consecutive runs. Both rows are measurements; the delta is their subtraction, nothing more.

**What changed between the two runs**: the cold tier, and nothing else. SAME database file, SAME binary, SAME machine, consecutive runs: between the two, `plume-daemon retention` columnarised into Parquet the days entirely older than the hot window (1,104,752 rows out of 1,440,007, i.e. 76.7 %), and the daemon was restarted with `PLUME_COLD_TIER=1`. WARNING: 57 of the 105 cold cells return a TRUNCATED answer (the union path hydrates at most `PLUME_QUERY_MAX`=5,000 rows) — their delta is NOT a gap in speed but a gap in work, and they are marked as such in the table. The subsection "Is the answer the SAME?" quantifies the content gap: up to x203 on a simple `stats count`. THIS RUN DESCRIBES THE CODE FROM BEFORE THE cold truncation FIX and it is kept for that reason: it is the MEASUREMENT of the defect. The run that describes the current repository is `chaud-seul-v2@1.4M` against `froid-actif-v2@1.4M`, below.

Machine load recorded: `loadavg` 2.5–3.7 during the BEFORE run, 1.9–3.9 during the AFTER run. On a shared machine, a gap of a few milliseconds proves nothing; only clear-cut gaps are usable, and the cells whose dispersion is annotated above are to be read with the same reservation.

**57 of these rows oppose answers with DIFFERENT content** (one side truncates): their delta measures a gap in work, not a gap in speed. They are marked.

105 comparable cells. A non-comparable cell is NOT a neutral result: it is absent on one side.

## Measured gap between two runs — `chaud-seul-v2@1.4M` vs `froid-actif-v2@1.4M`

Comparison `chaud-seul-v2@1.4M` -> `froid-actif-v2@1.4M`, SAME database, SAME instrument, SAME machine, consecutive runs. Both rows are measurements; the delta is their subtraction, nothing more.

**What changed between the two runs**: the cold tier AFTER the truncation fix, on the SAME database copies and the SAME machine as the previous run, with the post-fix binary. What changed in the product: (1) the columnar router is ARMED BY DEFAULT as soon as the cold tier is active — its DORMANT default was the measured cause of the defect: none of the 105 cold cells reached the kernels; (2) the guard "only route what the union path would return identically" no longer applies to AGGREGATES — beyond the hydration ceiling, the union path aggregates over a SAMPLE, and parity with a wrong number is not a virtue; (3) no value DERIVED from a truncated set can be serialised any more (`cold_store/exactness.rs`): failing to compute it exactly, the daemon REFUSES, naming its cause and the exact way (HTTP 422). MEASURED RESULT: the TRUNCATED cells go from 57 to 11, and the 11 remaining ones are ALL materialisations (`| table` / raw pages) — that is, the legitimate case: true rows, in incomplete number, flagged. 24 cells now answer 422: these are the forms that the columnar engine cannot compute exactly (dc(), free term, JSON field, group-by straddling the boundary). A 422 cell has no comparable latency: it measures a refusal, not work. CAUTION when reading the deltas: a cell that goes from "truncated" to "exact" does MORE work than before — a slowdown there is the price of correctness, not a regression.

Machine load recorded: `loadavg` 2.6–3.8 during the BEFORE run, 1.5–5.2 during the AFTER run. On a shared machine, a gap of a few milliseconds proves nothing; only clear-cut gaps are usable, and the cells whose dispersion is annotated above are to be read with the same reservation.

81 comparable cells. A non-comparable cell is NOT a neutral result: it is absent on one side.

## The windows measured, and those that are not

The windows are not chosen: they are DERIVED from two product parameters — the
hot window (`PLUME_COLD_HOT_WINDOW_DAYS`, default **7 d**, `cold_store/aging.rs`) and the
retention (`PLUME_RETENTION_DAYS`) — then filtered by the actual span of the dataset.

| Window | What it measures |
|---|---|
| `1h` | last hour |
| `24h` | last day |
| `7d` | the product's hot window (7 d) |
| `au-dela-7d` | beyond the hot window (from -28 d to -7 d) |
| `all` | all |

**Windows excluded by the coverage guard — hence NOT MEASURED**:

- `30d` (the whole retention (30 d)) — the dataset only spans 28 d: this window would be `all` under a 30 d label

A window wider than the dataset does not measure what its label says: it measures
`all` under another name. The harness refuses to fire it rather than publish a cell
whose title would be wrong. To get it, a dataset that covers it is needed — that is,
filling over a longer span (`BENCH_SPAN_DAYS`), not making the guard more permissive.

## The cold tier — measured

With a hot window of 7 days and a retention of 365, `daemon/src/cold_store/` is
the read path for **358 of the 365 days** of a deployment. The tables above
all run at `PLUME_COLD_TIER=0`: they say nothing about this path. This section is
the only one that talks about it, and it only talks about what was fired.

**Measured columnarisation** (real path: `plume-daemon retention` -> `retention_run`
-> `cold_age_run`, hot window 7 d):

| | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| HOT rows (SQLite) | 1,440,007 | 335,255 |
| Hot database | 1434 MiB | 1434 MiB |
| Cold tier (encrypted Parquet) | 0 MiB | 101 MiB in 22 files |

**1,104,752 rows (76.7 %) left SQLite for Parquet**, in 22 files (one per day). The cold side weighs **96 bytes per event** where the hot side occupied 1044 (table, indexes and FTS included), i.e. **11x more compact**.

> Duration: 2597 s = MEASURED interval between the timestamps of the first and the last Parquet file written (22 files, one per day). The run was then INTERRUPTED by a kill EXTERNAL to the product during the hot deletion phase, then RESUMED by a second `plume-daemon retention` which finished in ~90 s and returned "rétention OK": the aging restarted without loss, which is its contract (two phases, idempotent). The total duration is therefore NOT a clean columnarisation throughput, and is not published as such.

### Is the answer the SAME? (measured parity)

A latency is comparable only if both paths return the same answer: a
path that TRUNCATES is faster because it does less. This subsection therefore does not
compare times, it compares **the values returned**.

Method: SAME database, two copies: one columnarised (PLUME_COLD_TIER=1, 335,255 hot rows + 1,104,752 in Parquet), the other intact (PLUME_COLD_TIER=0, 1,440,007 hot rows). SAME binary, SAME machine, SAME queries, SAME windows. The VALUES RETURNED are compared, not the times: a latency is comparable only if the answer is.

| Query | Window | Without cold tier | With cold tier | Gap | Truncated? |
|---|:--:|---:|---:|---:|:--:|
| `search source=auditd severity>=2 \| stats count` | au-dela-7d | **58,747** | **289** | x203.3 | **yes** (5,000 rows hydrated) |
| `search source=auditd severity>=2 \| stats count` | all | **78,314** | **18,325** | x4.3 | **yes** (5,000 rows hydrated) |

The hot∪cold union path hydrates the cold side into a temporary SQLite table bounded
at `PLUME_QUERY_MAX` rows (default **5,000**, `cold_store/reader.rs:130`) then aggregates
OVER THIS SAMPLE. The count returned is therefore not "approximate": it is **wrong by a
factor that depends on the volume of the window**. The daemon FLAGS it
(`stats.truncated=true`), but a reader who only looks at the number sees a wrong
number. Any "cold" latency of this run must therefore be read with its
"truncated" column: when it says yes, the cell measures the time of an INCOMPLETE answer,
and cannot be compared with the hot cell.

> Caveat: A THIRD query was fired (`search | stats count by source,severity`, window au-dela-7d): both sides served it through the ROLLUP ROUTE, without truncation, but their values diverge by a factor of ~6.6 (the intact copy returns ~160 k events in total, the columnarised one ~1.05 M — the latter being consistent with the expected volume of the window). This divergence IS NOT EXPLAINED by this measurement. Candidate mechanism, to be settled by a dedicated experiment: the freshness of `event_rollup`, which the rollup loop (120 s) and `retention_run` feed — the daemon of the intact copy had just started, that of the columnarised copy had been running for 20 minutes AND had seen a full `retention_run` go by. Until this is settled, no conclusion is drawn from this third query.

### Is the answer the SAME? (measured parity)

A latency is comparable only if both paths return the same answer: a
path that TRUNCATES is faster because it does less. This subsection therefore does not
compare times, it compares **the values returned**.

Method: BEFORE the fix. SAME database of 1,440,007 events, two copies: one columnarised (PLUME_COLD_TIER=1, 335,255 hot rows + 1,104,752 in 22 Parquet files), the other intact (PLUME_COLD_TIER=0). SAME pre-fix binary (bin:0642474ceedfaf15), SAME machine, SAME queries, SAME windows — the measure.py matrix, in full.

| Verdict | n | what it means |
|---|---:|---|
| `same` | 52 | both sides return the SAME answer. |
| `differs` | 4 | they diverge **without saying so** — a wrong number, readable and copyable. It is THE serious case. |
| `declared` | 49 | they diverge and the cold side SAYS so (`truncated`, or coverage note). The incompleteness becomes information. |
| `refused` | 0 | one side REFUSES, with a named reason. An error is better than a wrong number: it is the fallback position, not the failure. |

`declared` acquits nothing: a truncated AGGREGATE remains a wrong number, declared or not.
The categories never add up to an "all is well".

**The count that counts: 36 WRONG NUMBER(S).** It is the number of checks whose
answer carries a value computed OVER THE SET (`count`/`dc`/`stats … by …`) and whose
two sides DIVERGE — whether the cold side declared it or not. It is exactly what
the invariant of `cold_store/exactness.rs` forbids. The other categories describe
partial answers of ROWS (true, incomplete, flagged) or reasoned refusals:
they are not of the same order of severity.

> Count: Verdicts and WRONG NUMBER count RE-DERIVED with the current classifier from the STORED `hot`/`cold` answers, which are the measurement. Without this re-derivation, the two runs would be counted by two different rules and their comparison would mean nothing. No answer was re-measured.

**No scalar aggregate diverges.** The checks reducible to a number return
the same value on both sides, or else the cold side REFUSES to answer, naming its
cause. This is the invariant of `cold_store/exactness.rs`: no value derived from a
truncated set is returned as a number.

> Caveat: THE 3 WRONG NUMBERS THAT REMAIN ARE NOT THOSE OF THE COLD TIER. They are all carried by the SAME class, `C3b-groupby-routable` (`search | stats count by source,severity`), and both sides serve it through the ROLLUP ROUTE, not through the cold path. Measured over the `au-dela-7d` window, on the SAME data: the sum of the counts is 164,165 on the side WITHOUT the cold tier (`approx:false`, `truncated:false` — hence presented as EXACT) and 1,082,346 on the side WITH it (`approx:true`, with its note). The RAW count of the same window, measured on both sides by `search | stats count`, is 1,080,321. It is therefore the rollup route on the side WITHOUT the cold tier that UNDER-counts by a factor of 6.6, while declaring itself exact — a second defect of the same family (a wrong number without warning), DISTINCT from the cold truncation, NOT fixed here, and reproducible: a restored database whose `event_rollup` does not cover the deep past serves under-counted dashboards. The caveat of the 07/31 run left this mechanism "unexplained"; it now is explained, and it remains open.

### Is the answer the SAME? (measured parity)

A latency is comparable only if both paths return the same answer: a
path that TRUNCATES is faster because it does less. This subsection therefore does not
compare times, it compares **the values returned**.

Method: AFTER the rollup COVERAGE fixes (event_rollup AND event_dim_rollup, see daemon/src/rollup_coverage.rs). SAME bench database of 1440007 events, two FRESH copies of the same file: one columnarised (PLUME_COLD_TIER=1, 330255 hot rows + 1109752 in 22 Parquet files), the other intact (PLUME_COLD_TIER=0). SAME measurement binary (bin:80a19382ef3d30b8), SAME machine, SAME queries, SAME windows — the full measure.py matrix, produced by bench/parity.py (replayable). The columnarisation was produced by a release build of tree efd39e5; the aging code (cold_age_run) is identical in the measurement binary. BOTH daemons TICKED before the measurement and the publication of their coverage (event_rollup_cov_id) was VERIFIED on both sides — the previous run itself noted that one of the daemons had just started while the other had been running for twenty minutes, an uncontrolled factor which is eliminated here.

| Verdict | n | what it means |
|---|---:|---|
| `same` | 62 | both sides return the SAME answer. |
| `differs` | 7 | they diverge **without saying so** — a wrong number, readable and copyable. It is THE serious case. |
| `declared` | 12 | they diverge and the cold side SAYS so (`truncated`, or coverage note). The incompleteness becomes information. |
| `refused` | 24 | one side REFUSES, with a named reason. An error is better than a wrong number: it is the fallback position, not the failure. |

`declared` acquits nothing: a truncated AGGREGATE remains a wrong number, declared or not.
The categories never add up to an "all is well".

**The count that counts: 2 WRONG NUMBER(S).** It is the number of checks whose
answer carries a value computed OVER THE SET (`count`/`dc`/`stats … by …`) and whose
two sides DIVERGE — whether the cold side declared it or not. It is exactly what
the invariant of `cold_store/exactness.rs` forbids. The other categories describe
partial answers of ROWS (true, incomplete, flagged) or reasoned refusals:
they are not of the same order of severity.

**No scalar aggregate diverges.** The checks reducible to a number return
the same value on both sides, or else the cold side REFUSES to answer, naming its
cause. This is the invariant of `cold_store/exactness.rs`: no value derived from a
truncated set is returned as a number.

> Caveat: THE ×6.6 DIVERGENCE OF THE PREVIOUS RUN IS FIXED, AND IT IS THIS RUN THAT MEASURES IT. The caveat of `parity-apres-2026-07-31` described the binary from BEFORE the rollup coverage fix; it no longer describes the repository. Measured here, on the SAME database and at the SAME moment as the matrix (the RAW count being `search | stats count` on the SAME daemon): on the side WITHOUT the cold tier, `search | stats count by source,severity` returns 1,080,321 over the `au-dela-7d` window, 359,679 over `7d` and 1,440,007 over `all` — i.e. EXACTLY the raw count of the three windows, where the previous run returned 164,165 under `approx:false` for 1,080,321 real ones. The number of groups now matches on both sides (68/68, 63/63, 70/70; it was 59 against 68). WHAT REMAINS, AND IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: 2 checks still diverge, both `C3b-groupby-routable`, and it is the side WITH the cold tier that OVER-counts — 1,082,346 against 1,080,321 (+2,025, i.e. +0.19 %) over `au-dela-7d`, 360,020 against 359,679 (+341, i.e. +0.09 %) over `7d`. That side declares itself `approx:true` and carries its note; the side without the cold tier is `approx:false` and exact. The cause is the DOCUMENTED residue of `plan_merge`: below the hot/cold boundary, `event` is aged into Parquet, so a sub-hour HEAD partial cannot be scanned raw and is FOLDED into the rollup body, which covers the whole hour — the bench's `au-dela-7d` window starts at 1782990828, not aligned to the hour, and the fold adds the slice [1782990000, 1782990828). It is therefore not a leftover of the fixed defect: it is the hourly grain, bounded to a sub-hour sliver, and announced. WHY THESE 2 ARE STILL COUNTED AS WRONG NUMBERS: the classifier NEVER redeems a diverging aggregate because it is declared (`declared n'acquitte rien`). The rule is kept as is — loosening it to bring the count down to zero would be changing the rule after seeing the result.

"went through cold": it comes from `stats.cold` returned by the daemon, not from
the configuration label). **11 cells are TRUNCATED**: the union path hydrates the cold side into SQLite with a row ceiling (`PLUME_QUERY_MAX`, default 5,000, `cold_store/reader.rs:130`) — beyond it, the answer is PARTIAL and the daemon says so. An aggregate over a wide cold window is therefore not exact by default: it is the most important result of this section.

## The number of machines — what the single-host profile was hiding

The profiled database is **single-node**: all its sources have `distinct_hosts: 1`. `host`
being one of the six indexed columns, any cell that filters or groups by host there bears
on a **degenerate case of cardinality 1**. The runs below replay the same classes
on derived FLEET profiles (`bench/make_fleet_profile.py`), **at equal event
volume**.

**What exactly changes between these runs** — it must be said before reading the table:
**(1)** the cardinality of `host` (1, then N); **(2)** the MIX of sources, because
multiplying the host-local sources by N changes their relative weight (`auditd` goes from
38.5 % to 44.7 % of the stream). Both come from the same derivation. A class that moves
can therefore move for one OR the other reason — except the `C6*` classes, which name `host`
in the query: those isolate the cardinality, and they are the ones to read to
judge the genericity gap.

**What the fleet size changes in VOLUME** — derived (`bench/make_fleet_profile.py`)
from the distributions MEASURED per source, over the window of the profiled database:

| Hosts | Host-local sources | Single-host events (measured) | Fleet events (derived) | Factor |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 20 of 32 | 1,395,968 | 1,395,968 | x1.0 |
| 50 | 20 of 32 | 1,395,968 | 60,183,032 | x43.112 |
| 200 | 20 of 32 | 1,395,968 | 240,143,432 | x172.026 |

The "derived" column is NOT a measurement: it is the multiplication of the weight of the
sources declared host-local by the number of machines. What is measured is
the distribution of each source; what is declared is the list of
host-local sources (`bench/fleet-per-host.txt`, one row per source, with its reason).

A class whose latency does not move with the number of machines does not depend on the
cardinality of `host`. A class that moves is a class whose figures published on
a single-host profile **do not hold** for a fleet — and the direction of the error is not
always the same: where `host` serves as a FILTER, the single host is PESSIMISTIC (the filter there
selects everything, whereas it selects 1/N on a fleet); where `host` serves as a
GROUPING key, it is OPTIMISTIC (a single group instead of N). A single-host profile therefore does not
"flatter" the product: it describes it WRONGLY, in both directions at once.

## Genericity — the same queries on OTHER data profiles

A figure measured on our profile proves OUR case, not the general case. The runs below
replay **the same matrix** on profiles that differ from the witness by **a single**
parameter of the dataset, **at equal event volume**, on the same machine and the same
binary. Each axis is DERIVED from a decision of the execution path — not chosen for
the occasion: what decides index or scan, rollup route or sweep, hot or cold.

| Run | Axis | Value | What the profile says BEFORE -> AFTER | Events | Database (MiB) |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| `temoin-64h@0.6M` | **witness** | — | — | 600,003 | 647 |
| `flotte-1h-v2@0.6M` | hosts | 1 | cardinality of `host` = 1 | 600,003 | 634 |
| `flotte-50h-v2@0.6M` | hosts | 50 | cardinality of `host` = 50 | 600,003 | 377 |
| `card-haute@0.6M` | ext_card_scale | 25.0 | median cardinality 4 -> 100 | 600,003 | 649 |
| `sev-haute@0.6M` | severity_shift | 0.6 | severity >= 3 0.064 -> 0.4768 | 600,003 | 649 |
| `temoin-bis@0.6M` | **witness** | — | — | 600,003 | 656 |
| `taille-grande@0.6M` | event_size_scale | 3.0 | bytes/event 252.8 -> 758.2 | 600,003 | 1039 |

### Noise first — otherwise no gap can be interpreted

The witness was measured **twice**, on the **same database**, with the same binary and the
same machine — `temoin-64h@0.6M` then `temoin-bis@0.6M`. Nothing changes between them: neither the data, nor the code,
nor the setting. The two runs BRACKET the campaign (one at the start, the other at the end),
so the band also contains the drift of the machine during the campaign. The ratio
from one run to the other, cell by cell, is pure NOISE, and it is:

| Cells | min | 5 % | median | 95 % | max |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 105 | x0.07 | x0.51 | x0.92 | x1.80 | x29.82 |

**This is the yardstick.** The criterion retained below is the FULL RANGE `[x0.07,
x29.82]` — the more conservative of the two: a gap is declared attributable to the
profile only if it falls outside everything the repetition produced without anything being
changed. The quantiles are published alongside so that the reader sees whether the band is wide
because of ONE cell or of all of them.

This band is not a chosen threshold: it is a measurement. It widens by itself if
the machine is more loaded, and the document then concludes LESS. This is the intended
behaviour — a bench must lose conclusions when it loses conditions, never gain
confidence. **Caveat to know**: the fastest cells (close to the fixed cost
of a query, measured by `C0-plancher`) have a high relative noise while their stake
is nil; they widen the band and therefore make the test STRICTER, never looser.

A high share means: **on this axis, our figures do not transpose**. A third party whose
dataset differs from ours on this parameter will not get our latencies, and the gap is not a
measurement artefact since it falls outside the band measured on an identical repetition.

## The 2 GiB budget

Highest peak RSS observed, all cells combined: **1097 MiB** (53.5 % of the 2 GiB budget).

**No cell exceeded 2 GiB**, and this is not a deduction: the daemon ran
in a `MemoryMax=2G MemorySwapMax=0` scope, where an overrun results in a kernel kill,
not in swap. It was not killed.

## Concurrency — what the node does when the team works at the same time

Everything else in this document is taken **one query at a time**: no query waits for
its turn there, and the document said so itself. This section measures the other condition, the
real one: several analysts launching **very large** queries at the same time, on the
same database and under the **same enforced budget** of 2 GiB.

**A level** = *N* independent analysts (each with its own HTTP connection, each with its own
`viewer` account), each going through the mix several times, offsetting its starting point — two
neighbours therefore never fire the same query at the same instant. The level ends when all have
finished their work: the aggregate throughput is work ACTUALLY served, not an extrapolation.

**The order of the questions is deliberate: correctness first.** Three correctness defects
have just been found in the aggregate paths of this product, and none was visible on
a latency bench. Each concurrent answer is therefore compared **by its value** to the answer
obtained alone — same database, same binary, same window — before a single timing is looked at.

### The mix, and why it is this one

The mix is not a list of preferences: it is **derived from the solo run that
precedes it**. The FLOOR is the cheapest query observed (`C0-plancher`,
0.7 ms) — it is the FIXED cost of a query, not base work.
Each **family** of the matrix (the classes `C1`…`C6` of this document) enters through its
most expensive representative, and only if it costs at least **10 ×**
the floor. The floor's family thus fails its own test and excludes itself.
The floor is then added **separately**: it loads nothing, it measures what becomes of the
instant click of a dashboard while colleagues launch monsters.

| Class retained | Family | What it is | Cost ALONE (p50) |
|---|:--:|---|---:|
| `C1b-scan-agg-dc` | 1 | filtered scan + dc() on a real column | 7315 ms |
| `C2b-regex-msg` | 2 | regex on message (REGEXP, Rust UDF) | 4053 ms |
| `C3-groupby-hi` | 3 | group-by 3 high-cardinality dims (src_ip,host,source) | 9539 ms |
| `C4b-raw-deep` | 4 | RAW paginated deep page (offset 200,000) | 348 ms |
| `C5-regex-json-planted` | 5 | regex on planted EXTENDED field (fields.needle) | 4825 ms |
| `C6b-groupby-host` | 6 | group-by on host (as many groups as machines) | 332 ms |
| `C0-plancher` | 0 | FLOOR: seek on a non-existent source (0 rows) | 0.7 ms |

Families **excluded** from the heavy mix, with their measured reason:

- family 0 (`C0-plancher`): the most expensive of family 0 is only 1.0 x the floor (threshold 10).

**Settling before measuring**: a daemon that has just started launches a full `ANALYZE`
in the background, which takes the write lock and consumes disk and CPU —
measuring right away means measuring the startup.
The harness therefore waits for 3 consecutive shots whose pre-engine wait is
under one millisecond: **10.0 s** here
(`quiescent=true`).

Columns: *duration* = wall time of the whole level; *throughput* = queries served per second
(in parentheses, the ratio to level 1 of the same run); *p50/p95/worst* cover
**all** queries of the level; *p50 of the worst analyst* is the worst of the individual
medians — it is the one that says whether the load is fair; *PERMIT wait* is the time
spent queuing at the semaphore, and NOTHING else (the time spent waiting for the lock
of the shared connection is published separately, below); *ceiling hit* is the
cgroup counter `memory.events:max`, that is, the number of times the kernel had to
reclaim memory to stay under 2 GiB during this level.

*Load the daemon, not the machine*: the instrument itself never consumed more than
**1.1 %** of a core-second per second of measurement on this run — the measured
latency is therefore not its own. The daemon, for its part, is locked in its cgroup at 2 GiB
without swap: the two pressures are recorded separately (`pressure_*` in the JSONL).

Columns: *duration* = wall time of the whole level; *throughput* = queries served per second
(in parentheses, the ratio to level 1 of the same run); *p50/p95/worst* cover
**all** queries of the level; *p50 of the worst analyst* is the worst of the individual
medians — it is the one that says whether the load is fair; *PERMIT wait* is the time
spent queuing at the semaphore, and NOTHING else (the time spent waiting for the lock
of the shared connection is published separately, below); *ceiling hit* is the
cgroup counter `memory.events:max`, that is, the number of times the kernel had to
reclaim memory to stay under 2 GiB during this level.

*Load the daemon, not the machine*: the instrument itself never consumed more than
**1.4 %** of a core-second per second of measurement on this run — the measured
latency is therefore not its own. The daemon, for its part, is locked in its cgroup at 2 GiB
without swap: the two pressures are recorded separately (`pressure_*` in the JSONL).

### Waiting for a permit, separated from what is not

It is the `sem_wait_ms` field that the daemon publishes to separate "the query is slow" from
"the query was waiting for its turn". The previous campaign showed **that it did not do so**,
and the demonstration required no threshold: as long as there are **at least as many permits as
analysts**, no query can wait for its turn. At these levels, waiting for a permit
is zero *by construction* — any non-zero value there is necessarily something else.

**Before the split**: the maximum observed where no queue is possible is
**10.2 s** under sub-critical load, and **16.5 s** during the
solo run (a single client, no other in flight). A semaphore with free permits cannot
produce that: the field measured something other than its name, and its name sends
the operator to RAISE the semaphore — the only action that the previous section measures
as harmful (throughput ×0.46, p95 27 s → 50 s, RSS +725 MiB, daemon killed at 10 analysts).

**After: zero everywhere.** Where no queue is possible, the published wait is zero —
not "small": zero, at the microsecond resolution of the field. This is not a measurement
that happened to land right: when a permit is free it is taken without ever
suspending the task, and the published value is the CONSTANT zero
(`daemon/src/query_timing.rs`) — no clock is involved on this path, so nothing
can contaminate it. The property "as many permits as clients ⇒ no wait" has
ceased to be a measurement to check and become the construction of the value, and the
harness EXITS WITH AN ERROR if it is violated instead of publishing the figure.

#### Where the time goes, now that it is split

The field could not be fixed by moving it: what it added up had to be
**separated**, otherwise the hidden part would simply have fallen elsewhere. The daemon therefore publishes
a TOTAL split — `prepare + sem_wait + exec == server` by construction, `exec` being the
remainder and never a third clock:

| field | what it measures |
|---|---|
| `prepare_ms` | before the permit: body, masks, **rollup coverage**, compilation |
| `sem_wait_ms` | the PERMIT wait, and nothing else |
| `db_lock_wait_ms` | the time spent **obtaining** the lock of the SHARED connection (not the time spent holding it) |
| `exec_ms` | the remainder: execution |

**The serialisation nobody saw.** The path of an interactive query reads the
rollup coverage. As long as this read took the lock of the
**shared** connection — the very one that the rollup loop holds for a whole tick
(`spawn_rollup_loop`, 120 s) and that the startup `ANALYZE` holds for several minutes —
**no semaphore bounded this wait**: it happened somewhere other than on the
semaphore, and raising the semaphore only puts more people into it.

MEASURED, lock in place (`conc-sem3-attribue@1.4M`):
up to **4.1 s** under load and **3.4 s** solo — on the
path of EVERY GXQL query, while the permit wait, for its part, was zero.

MEASURED after removal (`conc-sem3-corrige@1.4M`, `conc-sem8-corrige@1.4M`):
**zero**. The coverage read moved to the read pool — same committed `meta`
rows, same fail-closed fallback to "nothing established", hence the same rollup body
served or declined; only the lock disappears. The field is still published at zero: a missing
field would read "I do not know", a zero reads "I looked".

It is the reading that changes a decision: an operator who sees the permit wait at
zero and the shared lock non-zero knows that their semaphore is not the lever. Before the
split, both were in the same field, under the name of the semaphore.

**No route in a blind spot**: all the classes fired here publish their split,
including the `/api/search` bar, which takes a permit on the SAME semaphore and published
nothing at all until the previous campaign. A route invisible to the concurrency measurement
still weighs on it: it consumes the same permits.

### The 2 GiB budget, with several users

- **Daemon peak RSS, all levels combined: 2045 MiB** (100 % of the budget).
- **Peak cgroup memory: 2048 MiB** for a ceiling of 2048 MiB.
  This is not the same quantity as the RSS: the kernel compares the CGROUP memory to the ceiling,
  page cache included. A 1.4 GiB database read in a loop fills it — the cgroup therefore lives
  **pressed against its ceiling**, and what varies is not its occupancy but its reclaim
  work.
- **THE BUDGET GAVE WAY**: `conc-sem8@1.4M`, **10 analysts** (semaphore 8). Peak RSS 2045 MiB against a ceiling of 2048 MiB, 62 queries out of 210 did not complete, and the process no longer existed at the end of the level. Under `MemoryMax` **without swap**, this cannot be anything other than a budget overrun: the kernel kills, it does not slide into swap. The levels beyond are **not** measured — an absence, not a zero.
- The degradation is not binary: BEFORE the kill, the daemon first cleanly REFUSED queries, naming its cause (interactive budget of 60 s exceeded, `4xx`). The named refusal therefore comes first; the kill is what follows when memory, for its part, does not negotiate.
- **Killed by the kernel (`memory.events:oom_kill`): 0** — cgroup counter, to be read with the reservation above: the cgroup of a killed scope disappears with it, and its counter is then no longer readable at all.
- The harness STOPPED the sweep after level 10 (`conc-sem8@1.4M`): the daemon no longer exists after this level: under MemoryMax without swap, this means a BUDGET OVERRUN (kernel kill). The following levels are NOT measured.

### What the semaphore size costs, and what it brings

The interactive semaphore is at 3 by default, after having been lowered from 8 **as a
RAM lever**. The runs compared here run on the SAME database, the SAME machine, the
SAME binary **and the SAME query mix**: their gap, at an equal number of analysts,
IS the exchange rate between concurrency and memory.

**It can be tuned without recompiling**: `PLUME_QUERY_CONCURRENCY` is read from the
configuration at startup (`daemon/src/server/mod.rs`, default 3) and the daemon publishes the
value it applies on `/api/system/diag` — that is where this bench reads it, rather than
assuming it. On the other hand it is read **only once, at boot**: changing it requires a
restart, and a restart has its own cost (see the settling above).

**Excluded from this comparison**: `conc-sem3@1.4M`, `conc-sem8@1.4M`, `conc-sem3-rouge@1.4M`, `conc-sem3-attribue@1.4M`
— their mix OR their binary is not that of the other runs, so their throughput
gap would be attributable not to the semaphore but to the work or the code. Their curve
remains published above; it is this comparison, and it alone, that requires that
everything else be identical.

These six numbers ARE the exchange rate between a semaphore at 3 and a semaphore at 8 — the one that the lowering from 8 to 3, made as a RAM lever, had bought without ever being quantified.

## How latency rises with volume

Measured at several volumes, empty mask, `PLUME_FTS_FIELDS=0`, window "all". It is the slope that answers the "millions of events" question, not an isolated point.

**WHAT THESE COLUMNS DO NOT HOLD FIXED** — derived from the records themselves, not declared by hand, because a comparability sentence that one WRITES is a sentence that one no longer measures:

- `cold`: **2 distinct values** across the columns. The gap read from one column to the next is therefore NOT attributable to volume alone.
- `profile`: **4 distinct values** across the columns. The gap read from one column to the next is therefore NOT attributable to volume alone.
- `version`: **7 distinct values** across the columns. The gap read from one column to the next is therefore NOT attributable to volume alone.
- **600,003, 1,440,007**: several columns share this volume. Two columns at the SAME volume are not two points of the axis — what separates them is, by construction, something other than volume.

Caveat to know before citing this table: the volumes come from **distinct runs**, hence from distinct databases and possibly different numbers of repetitions (the `reps` column of the raw JSONL says so cell by cell). The points are comparable in order of magnitude, not to the percent. An empty cell = class not measured at this volume. **The ratio in the last column opposes the FIRST and the LAST**: it inherits everything listed above.

A class whose latency ratio follows the row ratio is a **scan**: its cost is linear in volume and nothing indexes it. A class whose ratio stays flat is served by an index or by a rollup.

⚠ **floor-bound base**: at the small volume, the cell was already at the fixed floor (~51 ms, see `C0-plancher`). The ratio shown then measures the distance to this floor, NOT the slope of the scan — do not cite it as a scaling factor.

## Levers designated by the measurement

None is implemented here: it is the role of the instrument to **designate** them and to quantify
the gain one would be entitled to expect from them. Ranked by decreasing measured gain. "RAM cost"
says what the lever would add to the 2 GiB budget; when it is nil, it is written.

### L1. Make the rollup route compatible with masking

*Measured gain: **36.1 s** at p50 on the most telling cell (`fts0-masque-vide@1.4M` vs `fts0-masque-non-vide@1.4M`). This is not a promise of gain: it is the gap THAT THE MEASUREMENT SHOWS today between the slow path and a fast path that already exists or is reachable.*

the SAME group-by, the SAME role: **152 ms** empty mask (served from `rollup`, 63 rows) against **36.3 s** non-empty mask (served from `raw`, 70 rows — the counts differ because the rollup route is APPROXIMATE, `stats.approx=true`: it is the price of its speed), i.e. **239.5x slower**. The confidentiality safeguard is therefore also a performance brake: a non-empty mask disarms the rollup route (`handlers/query.rs:282`) because `event_rollup` stores `src_ip`/`host` in plaintext. Two ways forward: mask when reading the rollup, or materialise one rollup per mask class. **RAM cost: that of an additional set of rollups** (on the reference installation, `event_rollup` weighs on the order of a MiB per million events, hence marginal), plus on-the-fly masking. The two runs opposed are `fts0-masque-vide@1.4M` and `fts0-masque-non-vide@1.4M`: they agree on EVERYTHING the reading declares — binary, number of events, database, cold tier — except masking. This is the only reason why this gap can be attributed to the mask.

### L2. Make the host index usable WITH a time bound

*Measured gain: **22.1 s** at p50 on the most telling cell (C6b 7d vs all). This is not a promise of gain: it is the gap THAT THE MEASUREMENT SHOWS today between the slow path and a fast path that already exists or is reachable.*

the SAME `stats count by host`, the SAME database: **102 ms** without a time bound against **22.2 s** bounded to the product's hot window (`7d`), i.e. **217x slower**. Without a bound, the group-by is served by an index-only scan (`idx_event_host` covers the query). As soon as a `ts` bound comes in, the host index is no longer enough — each row must be opened to read its `ts` — and the query becomes a scan again. Yet the time bound is the NORMAL case: a dashboard always looks at a window. Way forward: a composite index `(host, ts)`, which makes the time predicate satisfiable within the index. **RAM cost: nil; DISK cost: one more index** (on the reference installation, `idx_event_host` weighs a few tens of MiB per million events). Note: this cell is already at 64 hosts; on a fleet, the number of groups only grows.

### L3. Extend the rollup route to high-cardinality dimensions

*Measured gain: **14.1 s** at p50 on the most telling cell (C3-groupby-hi / all). This is not a promise of gain: it is the gap THAT THE MEASUREMENT SHOWS today between the slow path and a fast path that already exists or is reachable.*

`stats count by src_ip,host,source` over the whole history: **14.2 s**, served by `raw`. Only the `by` forms whose dimensions ALL fit in `{source, severity}` are routable (`rollup_route.rs:349-366`); as soon as a high-cardinality dimension comes in, it falls back to the scan. **RAM cost: that of the chosen grain** — a rollup at `src_ip` grain is bounded at execution by `PLUME_ROLLUP_SRCIP_TOPN` (50) precisely so as not to explode, which makes the result approximate. The exactness/memory trade-off must be decided, not endured.

### L4. The non-indexed extended field has no access path

*Measured gain: **6.1 s** at p50 on the most telling cell (C5b vs C5c). This is not a promise of gain: it is the gap THAT THE MEASUREMENT SHOWS today between the slow path and a fast path that already exists or is reachable.*

regex on `fields.object` (no index): **6.1 s** against **1.1 ms** for an equality on `fields.user`, which has a partial expression index. Only 12 fields are indexed (`HOT_FIELDS`, read from `daemon/src/soql_glue.rs`: action, user, owner, kind, ns, role, scope, verb, resource, operation, dir, risk) out of the **241 distinct keys of the measured profile**. For the 229 others, any search is a scan with `json_extract` per row. It is exactly the "on all fields" promise that is at stake. Ways forward: `event_fields_fts` (already written, see the lever on the cost of `PLUME_FTS_FIELDS`), or expression indexes on demand, or columnar storage of the fields. **RAM cost: one expression index per field**, to be arbitrated — and this arbitration has no automation today: the mechanism that promised to make it based on usage was removed (P6.8-b) without ever having promoted a single index.

### L5. Wire FTS5 into the GXQL path

*Measured gain: **3.1 s** at p50 on the most telling cell (C2c vs C2d). This is not a promise of gain: it is the gap THAT THE MEASUREMENT SHOWS today between the slow path and a fast path that already exists or is reachable.*

the same needle, the same number of rows returned: **3.1 s** through GXQL (`message LIKE '%…%'`, full scan) against **3.7 ms** through `/api/search` (FTS5 index `event_fts`). The index EXISTS and is already paid for — on the reference installation it weighs about six tenths of the weight of the table — but it is only wired into `/api/search`. On the GXQL path, a free term becomes `col LIKE '%motif%'` (`core/src/soql/dialect.rs:65-67`, called from `soql/mod.rs:881-891`), hence a full scan. **RAM cost: nil** — the index is already built and already in the database.

### L6. The cost of `PLUME_FTS_FIELDS=1`, and who benefits from it

*DISK effect measured on the ONLY pair that the property designates: **+11 %** of database (+138 MiB). This is not a gain, it is an expense — and the document says below who benefits from it, and what it costs ELSEWHERE than on disk.*

enabling `PLUME_FTS_FIELDS=1` took the database from **1263 MiB to 1401 MiB** (+138 MiB, +11 %), on the pair that the property designates: the run `fts1-masque-vide@1.4M` compared with ITS OWN size before the switch (`db_bytes_fts0`), hence on the same database, the same binary and the same number of events. Peak RSS, on the ONLY classes measured in both configurations (9), and on the SAME pair: **1072 MiB** at `FTS_FIELDS=0` (`fts0-masque-vide@1.4M`) against **691 MiB** at `FTS_FIELDS=1`. Caution: each configuration starts from a fresh daemon, so these two peaks did not have the same history to rise — the gap is NOT attributable to the flag alone, in either direction. The solid figure of this row is the DISK cost. Latency gap observed on the GXQL free term (whole history), on the SAME pair: **501 ms** to the detriment of FTS_FIELDS=1 — but this gap CANNOT come from the flag, since the GXQL path never reads `event_fields_fts`: it is measurement noise on a shared machine, and it is reported as such. THE COST THAT DECIDES IS NOT IN THIS BENCH, AND IT IS HEAVIER THAN THOSE ABOVE: the field index is declared WITHOUT A CONTENT TABLE, a form that the typed backup plan cannot recreate; each compressed cycle then falls back to an export that materialises a FULL DECRYPTED copy of the database, for the duration of the cycle. Enabling this capability is therefore a PERFORMANCE-FOR-CONFIDENTIALITY TRADE, and it is this reason — not a memory overhead, which this bench measures in neither direction — that justifies the default being off. Established by reading the sources, never by a run: see `docs/CHIFFREMENT-COMPRESSION.md` §3. Key point: `event_fields_fts` is only read by `/api/search` (`handlers/search.rs:146-157`). The GXQL path NEVER consults it — so its disk and ingest cost is paid without GXQL queries benefiting from it. It is the lever "Wire FTS5 into the GXQL path" that would make this already-accepted cost useful to GXQL queries.

## What is NOT measured here

- **The cold tier beyond what is fired**: 2 configuration(s) run
  `PLUME_COLD_TIER=1` (dedicated section above), but on ONE single hot window
  size and ONE single volume. The vectorised engine is not measured separately from the
  hydration path: the document does not say which one served each cell beyond what
  `stats.cold` reports about it.
- **Concurrency is measured** (dedicated section): up to 10 simultaneous
  analysts, semaphore 3 and 8. What remains outside the measurement:
  concurrency DURING an ingestion (the two loads are measured separately),
  SUSTAINED load over hours (each level lasts tens of seconds, not a
  day), and windows other than `all` — the
  mix is fired on the most expensive window, not on all of them.
- **Multi-tenancy** (`PLUME_MULTI_TENANT=1`): everything is measured in mode 0.
- **The cold page cache**: impossible to drop it without root privilege on the measurement
  machine. The `lu` column says what actually reached the disk; it does not say what
  a full cold start would do.
- **Text fidelity**: the message bodies are synthetic. The FTS5, `LIKE`
  and `REGEXP` figures depend directly on this vocabulary; it is the most serious limit of the
  bench and it is described in `bench/gen_events.py` (`VOCAB`).
- **Indexing of extended fields**: `PLUME_EXPRINDEX=1` (the shipped default) is the ONLY
  lever, and it only indexes the names in `HOT_FIELDS`. No mechanism indexes a field based on
  usage any more — the one that promised it was removed (P6.8-b) without ever having promoted an index.
  This table therefore CANNOT show an extended field outside this list served by an index:
  it is not an unmeasured cell, it is a cell that no configuration would fill.

## Reproduce, and contradict

```sh
# 1. the data profile (already versioned; to re-extract only for another deployment)
#    bench/prod-profile.sql, READ ONLY, extracts no row value
# 2. the full matrix, end to end:
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=../.bench-target cargo build --release --features cold_tier \
    --manifest-path daemon/Cargo.toml
bench/run.sh                       # 10 M events
BENCH_EVENTS=1000000 bench/run.sh  # 1 M, to iterate
# 2 bis. CONCURRENCY, on an already filled database (restarts the daemon for each
#        semaphore value and ASKS it again what it applies before measuring):
BENCH_PHASES=concurrency BENCH_SEM_SWEEP=3,8 BENCH_CONC_LEVELS=1,2,3,4,6,8,10 bench/run.sh
# 3. the rendering — THE EXACT COMMAND that produced THIS document, rebuilt from its own
#    arguments and pointed at the VERSIONED data (hence replayable by a third party):
python3 bench/report.py bench/results/results-smoke-200k.jsonl bench/results/results.jsonl bench/results/results-2026-07-31.jsonl bench/results/results-2026-07-31-corrige.jsonl bench/results/parity-avant-2026-07-31.jsonl bench/results/parity-apres-2026-07-31.jsonl bench/results/parity-couverture-2026-07-31.jsonl bench/results/concurrency-2026-08-01.jsonl bench/results/concurrency-reproduction-2026-08-01.jsonl bench/results/concurrency-attribution-2026-08-01.jsonl bench/results/concurrency-corrige-2026-08-01.jsonl bench/results/generique-2026-08-03.jsonl \
    --ingest-curve bench/results/ingest_rate.csv \
    --ingest-curve bench/results/ingest_rate-quiet-2g.csv \
    --ref chaud-seul-v2@1.4M \
    --compare avant-leviers@1.4M:apres-leviers@1.4M \
    --compare-note 'two fixes of the query path, measured here. (1) The budget guard now waits on a CONDITION (condvar with timeout) instead of polling a flag every 50 ms: it protects the same thing, at the same threshold, with the same interruption, but it no longer QUANTISES the latency — previously every reading was rounded up to the next multiple of 50 ms, and the guard was joined before the response was sent. It covers both execution gates: `run_on_conn` (/api/query) and `read_with_watchdog` (alerts, cases, freshness, sources, /api/search). (2) Whether cursor pagination applies is DERIVED from the properties of the wrap instead of a list of two commands, and a projected pipeline (`| table`/`| fields`) is now served by the cursor instead of silently falling back to OFFSET: this is the `C4d-keyset-projete` cell. Comparability caveat: these two runs use the SAME database, but AFTER the `event_fields_fts` fill of phase 3 (database 1434 MiB against 1263 MiB for the `fts0-*@1.4M` tables above) and on a much less loaded machine. They are comparable WITH EACH OTHER; they are not comparable with the tables of the first reference. Five cells go the other way (C1b/all +2.7 s, C5b/24h +632 ms, C5/all +467 ms, C2d/24h +252 ms): on these four the `SQL` column moves AS MUCH as the wall time, yet the fixes act ONLY on the wait AROUND the SQL — these are therefore long scans jostled by the machine, and they are left as they are.' \
    --compare chaud-seul@1.4M:froid-actif@1.4M \
    --compare-note 'the cold tier, and nothing else. SAME database file, SAME binary, SAME machine, consecutive runs: between the two, `plume-daemon retention` columnarised into Parquet the days entirely older than the hot window (1,104,752 rows out of 1,440,007, i.e. 76.7 %), and the daemon was restarted with `PLUME_COLD_TIER=1`. WARNING: 57 of the 105 cold cells return a TRUNCATED answer (the union path hydrates at most `PLUME_QUERY_MAX`=5,000 rows) — their delta is NOT a gap in speed but a gap in work, and they are marked as such in the table. The subsection "Is the answer the SAME?" quantifies the content gap: up to x203 on a simple `stats count`. THIS RUN DESCRIBES THE CODE FROM BEFORE THE cold truncation FIX and it is kept for that reason: it is the MEASUREMENT of the defect. The run that describes the current repository is `chaud-seul-v2@1.4M` against `froid-actif-v2@1.4M`, below.' \
    --compare chaud-seul-v2@1.4M:froid-actif-v2@1.4M \
    --compare-note 'the cold tier AFTER the truncation fix, on the SAME database copies and the SAME machine as the previous run, with the post-fix binary. What changed in the product: (1) the columnar router is ARMED BY DEFAULT as soon as the cold tier is active — its DORMANT default was the measured cause of the defect: none of the 105 cold cells reached the kernels; (2) the guard "only route what the union path would return identically" no longer applies to AGGREGATES — beyond the hydration ceiling, the union path aggregates over a SAMPLE, and parity with a wrong number is not a virtue; (3) no value DERIVED from a truncated set can be serialised any more (`cold_store/exactness.rs`): failing to compute it exactly, the daemon REFUSES, naming its cause and the exact way (HTTP 422). MEASURED RESULT: the TRUNCATED cells go from 57 to 11, and the 11 remaining ones are ALL materialisations (`| table` / raw pages) — that is, the legitimate case: true rows, in incomplete number, flagged. 24 cells now answer 422: these are the forms that the columnar engine cannot compute exactly (dc(), free term, JSON field, group-by straddling the boundary). A 422 cell has no comparable latency: it measures a refusal, not work. CAUTION when reading the deltas: a cell that goes from "truncated" to "exact" does MORE work than before — a slowdown there is the price of correctness, not a regression.' \
    --fill-log bench/results/fill-progress-quiet-2g.txt \
    --rendu-le '2026-09-09 16:15:55+0200' \
    --materiel '{"cpu": "Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-9750H CPU @ 2.60GHz", "cores": 12, "mem_gib": 15.4, "kernel": "7.1.8-zen1-3-zen"}' \
    --langue en -o docs/BENCHMARK.md
```

This command is **regenerated at each rendering**: it cannot drift out of sync with the
document. This is deliberate — the previous version published an incomplete command which, replayed
as is, AMPUTATED the document of its gap sections and its attribution tables.
A wrong reproduction command is worse than none: it makes one believe in a
successful reproduction.

The generator is deterministic: `python3 bench/gen_events.py --count N --end-ts T --digest`
prints the SHA-256 of the stream. Two executions with the same parameters give the same
fingerprint — this is what makes a disagreement on the figures arbitrable.
